opus-5.5.text:
Well, my first reaction was honestly something like, "Why me?" I'm a quantum computing person. I've spent most of my career thinking about what quantum computers can and can't do, about the foundations of complexity theory, and I'd always been a sort of interested bystander when it came to AI safety. I'd read the arguments and had friendly disagreements with people in the rationalist community going back years. But I didn't think of myself as someone with anything special to contribute.

When they first reached out, I think I told them something like, "I'm flattered, but I don't really see what a theoretical computer scientist could do here." Their answer was, more or less, "That's exactly what we want you to figure out." They weren't asking me to stop doing quantum computing. They offered a leave year where I could think about whether complexity theory had anything to say about making AI systems safer and more aligned.

That intrigued me, because a lot of the most interesting ideas in theoretical computer science came from people asking, "Can we put this vague, philosophical concern on a mathematical footing?" Cryptography is the classic example. People had intuitions about secrecy for thousands of years, and then in the 1970s and 80s someone said, "Let's define what it means for an encryption scheme to be secure, and prove things about it." I wondered whether something like that could happen with AI alignment. Could you formalize what it means for a model to be honest, or to not have a hidden backdoor, or for one system to verify the behavior of a more powerful one? That last question connects to interactive proofs, a weaker verifier checking claims made by a more powerful prover, which is really the heart of complexity theory.

So I went from skepticism to thinking, "Okay, there might be something here, and if there's even a chance, given how fast these systems are progressing, it would be strange to say no." And part of it was just that it was 2022, I'd been playing with GPT-3 and early versions of what became ChatGPT, and it was clear the world was changing. As a scientist you want to be where the action is, and I felt I'd regret not taking a closer look.

r001.rationale: He says his first reaction was “Why me?” because he was a quantum-computing researcher and did not think he had anything special to contribute to AI safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was a mix of skepticism and bemusement. I'm a quantum computing and computational complexity person. I'd spent twenty years thinking about things like whether P equals NP and what quantum computers can and can't do. When OpenAI reached out in 2022 and said, essentially, "come spend a year with us and think about what theoretical computer science can say about AI safety," my gut response was: I'm not sure it can say anything at all. I didn't want to be the guy who shows up, waves his hands about complexity classes, and produces nothing useful.

But a couple of things changed my mind. One was that this was clearly going to be the most important technological story of our lifetimes, and I'd been watching it from the sidelines, occasionally blogging about it, and I thought, if there's even a small chance that the tools I know could matter here, I'd regret not trying. The other was that I didn't have to pretend the problem was clean. They weren't asking me to prove a theorem that alignment is solvable. They were asking me to think, with some freedom, about whether there were pieces of the problem that could be made precise. And that's a much more honest invitation.

So I took a leave from UT Austin, and what I ended up spending most of my time on was watermarking, how you'd statistically mark the output of a language model so you could later detect that it came from the model, without changing the quality of the text. That's a problem where you can actually state what you want, prove something about it, and build it. Which was a relief, because a lot of the rest of AI safety is still, as far as I can tell, pre-paradigmatic. It's more like philosophy than like math. And I went in knowing I might come out of it with more questions than theorems.

r001.rationale: He identifies himself as a quantum computing and complexity researcher and says his first reaction was that he was unsure those tools could say anything useful about AI safety, conveying skepticism about why OpenAI invited him.
